lines: Picture a table with a freshness target of ninety-nine percent over a rolling thirty days.
Now its source goes stale for a real six hours. That's a genuine incident, not a blip.
Here's what I actually want you to commit to before I show you the answer.
Does a reasonable-looking alert catch that six-hour stall in the first five minutes, only after the whole budget's already gone, or not at all?
And separately, does that same alert also go off at four in the morning, every single night, just because the table is waiting on its own normal run?
answer: A plain fixed threshold genuinely can't tell those two situations apart. Both just look like the data is old.

What actually works is two separate pieces: a multi-window rule that catches the real outage within minutes, and a schedule-aware check that stops it from paging for a gap that was expected all along.

lines: Before any of the math, there's a principle underneath all of this, and it's worth saying plainly.
Alert on what the person reading the data actually experiences, not on every single internal thing that could have gone wrong along the way.
Because here's the real cost when you don't: every page has to earn the right to interrupt someone, or the next real one gets ignored right along with all the noise.
So, concretely, how fast is a budget actually being spent?
That's what burn rate measures, relative to the SLO itself.
A burn rate of exactly one means you're on pace to spend the whole thing right at the end of the window. Thirty days out, not a minute sooner.
Now watch what a plain fixed threshold actually does with that number.
A complete outage and a barely-noticeable one both trigger the alert after the exact same hour. There's no sense of how bad it actually is baked in anywhere.
And once it does fire, it can keep firing for most of the rest of that long window, long after whatever actually broke is already fixed.
The fix for that second problem is almost embarrassingly simple once you see it.
Put a much shorter window right next to the long one, sized at roughly a twelfth of it.
Run that same outage through it again, and it clears in minutes this time, not most of a month.
There are even specific numbers worth memorizing here, because they're a genuinely good starting point.
Two percent of the budget in one hour, five percent in six hours, and that's worth paging someone for. Ten percent over three days is more of a ticket.
But here's the honest catch nobody tells you up front: push the target low enough, and even a complete, full outage can sit under that page threshold and simply never trigger it at all.
One more wrinkle that's specific to data, and the SRE playbook on its own doesn't cover it.
A daily table is supposed to look nearly a full day old, right before it runs. That's not broken, that's just Tuesday.
A fixed age threshold pages for that every single night. Measure the age against when the table is actually expected to run instead, and that false alarm simply stops happening.
One failure upstream can light up every single signal downstream of it at the exact same moment.
Left alone, that's not one incident, it's ten separate pages for people who all needed the same one piece of information.
Group those into a single page, and send it to whoever actually owns the thing that broke.
Before any alert ships, run it through one honest question.
Can a person actually do something about this, right now, the moment it fires?
If the answer's no, it isn't a page. It's a ticket for tomorrow, or it's nothing at all.
Put all of that together and here's what a genuinely good alert actually looks like.

It watches the symptom, not every possible cause behind it. It has a short window sitting next to a long one. It knows the schedule, not just a fixed age. One incident gets exactly one page. And nothing pages at all unless someone can actually act on it.
Last one, and it's the kind of thing that actually happens on a real team.
A nightly freshness alert does its job and correctly catches a real six-hour outage. Then the very next morning, it fires again, for the table's own completely ordinary overnight gap.
What's the one change that actually fixes that, without also making the alert slower to catch the next real outage?
answer: Widening the window looks tempting, but it just trades one problem for another: now the real outage takes longer to catch too.
The actual fix is making the freshness check schedule-aware, so it's comparing age against when the table is supposed to run, not one fixed number.
Do that, and it stays fast on the real outage while finally going quiet on the ordinary nights.
